recentItems.description:

recentItems.title: Artificial snowmaking is key to Australia's ski industry future, says peak body | The Business
recentItems.description:
Snow Resorts Australia says Australia's winter snow economy is worth almost $6 billion, with more than two million visitors annually. 

But revenue is at risk of melting away, as the warmest winter on record ends the ski season early. Natural snow coverage on the Australian alps is among the lowest ever recorded.

The value of NSW resort, Thredbo, has been written down by half to $143 million from $292 million in 2022, as the parent company EVT considers selling it off along with a raft of other assets.

While the industry says investment in snowmaking helps mitigate the changing climate, average temperatures are on the rise.

Snow Resorts Australia chief executive, Josh Elliott is confident snowmaking will keep skiers returning.

"We've certainly had challenges in terms of natural snow conditions and mother nature hasn't provided as we hoped... Snowmaking has been more than a 35-year investment and as technology has adapted, Australian resorts have continued to invest and they've really been at the forefront of snow management for a number of years," he said.

recentItems.title: US bond market is like a 'slow moving car crash', says Michael McCarthy | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
Influential market strategist, Michael McCarthy says investors are concerned "an inflationary spiral will break out" and require "drastic action" to contain. He says that drastic action would be US interest rates at 8 per cent.

Speaking with Alicia Barry on The Business, Mr McCarthy said the bond market is still flashing a red warning about the financial system, despite the calming down a little overnight, as yields eased from multi-year highs on falling oil prices. 

In recent weeks, investors globally have bailed out of government bonds, sending yields spiking on worries about government debt levels, rising oil prices and inflation as well as the vast cash piles flowing into AI. 

The Moomoo Australia and New Zealand chief executive has previously warned about the risks of another global financial crisis originating in the United States on The Business.

In this interview, he talks about the risk of an inflationary spiral breaking out. "If people think that recessions are bad, wait until we see the return of inflation because the damage it did in the 1970s, it restructured economies, it destroyed businesses, it saw people out of work for years at a time. If we see inflation take off, that's the damage and destruction we're looking at," he says.

"It's very clear at the moment the trend is towards disaster and unless there is radical action it's going to be very hard to stop." 

When asked exactly what radical action would be needed, he says, "interest rates at 8 per cent... if US interest rates go to 8 per cent, Australian rates could go to 10 per cent.  This might mean that we're looking at a period of sustained higher interest rates to correct the imbalances that have arisen since the GFC."

recentItems.title: Why is Savers controversial? | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
Savers Australia is the subsidiary of US company Savers Value Village (SVV). The global retailer is worth $2.2 billion and has shares that trade on the New York Stock Exchange.  SVV is also North America's largest for-profit second-hand retailer with 185 stores in the US and 172 in Canada. Its 50 per cent gross profit margin is well above the industry average and the company earned more than $300 million last year, according to Refinitiv data.  

In Australia, Savers has 19 stores. It competes directly with non-profit, second-hand retailers Vinnies and Salvos, and smaller charity op shops that rely on selling donated goods to fund community programs.  Some of them are not happy about the expansion of Savers, concerned that its charity donation bins could potentially give it a veneer or "smoke screen" of being charitable. But the American head office of Savers told ABC News it gave its Australian non-profit partners $5.6 million last year.  Local boss Michael Fisher said "we partner with not-for-profit organisations.  They go and solicit donations from the general public, they bring them to the stores, and we pay them for those donations."  Diabetes Victoria boss Glen Noonan was at Savers's recent Geelong launch, where big green bins with his non-profit's logo were on proud display for people to donate into.  He said the millions it received last year from Savers was beneficial, and allowed Diabetes Victoria to revenue raise from second-hand donations without the grunt work of running shops themselves.

Michael Lasser, a retail analyst from investment bank UBS, which has done work for Savers, said its biggest overheads would be staff wages, store overheads and the undisclosed cost of buying used items.  "This is a business that is aimed at more effectively monetising the donated goods for charities," he said.  Like op shops and non-profit second-hand retailers, Savers also needs to deal with all of the donations from charity partners that it cannot sell in Australian stores.

recentItems.title: Accused Russian spies captured on prison audio | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
A series of audio recordings purporting to be with a Russian-born couple accused of spying on Australia have been published by Russian state-controlled media.
In the interviews, never reported in Australia before, former army private Kira Korolev and her husband, Igor, allegedly hit out at authorities over a lack of evidence.
Grace Tobin from ABC Investigations reports.
